## 2026-10-20 — install, its dry run and doctor stop waiting for a hung pi at a named limit and end every process that launch started

Spend served the current priority's installation line: nana working in terminal mode for both seats on macOS and Windows, installation included. Install and its dry run started `pi --version` and `pi install` through `stepPiRegister` in `packages/nana-setup/lib/steps.mjs`, and doctor started `pi --version` from diagnose in `lib/doctor.mjs`, each a spawnSync with no time limit. A pi stuck on a lock, the network or a broken install hung all three with no end. In the plan's probe on a hanging fake pi, install waited 6,370 ms and the dry run 6,036 ms, and both reported created and exit 0; doctor waited 6,091 ms and printed ✓ 1.0.2. The adversary's dry run was still waiting at 4 s. HANDOFF carried it as an install-dry-run-pi-packages residual. spawnSync's own timeout is not enough: it kills only its direct child, so a sh-wrapped fake pi's node survived, and on Windows cmd.exe dies while pi's node.exe stays.

**The change.** The new `lib/bounded-spawn.mjs` exports `boundedSpawnSync`, which returns spawnSync's shape and runs the launch through a relay, the new `lib/bounded-spawn-child.mjs`. The relay starts pi detached on POSIX, so pi leads its own group, and passes `windowsVerbatimArguments` through; neither the relay nor pi gets `windowsHide`. At the deadline it kills the tree: SIGKILL to the group on POSIX, taskkill with the pack's `TASKKILL_ARGS` on win32, falling back to the child alone. It reports one JSON line and exits, so a pi in uninterruptible sleep cannot hold it; the outer spawnSync waits the limit plus `RELAY_BACKSTOP_MS` (5 s) at most. `PI_LAUNCH_LIMITS_MS = { version: 30_000, install: 120_000 }` sits above `stepPiRegister` (chosen 2026-10-20: pi 1.0.2 answered in 0.15 s, and 30 + 2 × 120 = 270 s stays under the install check's 300 s). On a timeout, install and the dry run report pi packages ✗ `pi --version gave no answer within 30 s and was stopped` (or `pi install <dir> gave no answer within 120 s and was stopped`) and exit 1; doctor's pi executable row reads the same text plus the install hint, ✗ on the real home and a note under `--home`. Build 2 changed the signal path only: on SIGINT, SIGTERM or SIGHUP the relay passes the signal to pi's group, waits up to `RELAY_SIGNAL_GRACE_MS` (1 s, chosen) for pi to close, then kills the tree; a second signal kills at once, and on win32 it waits the same grace before taskkill. The deadline kill stays SIGKILL at once. Windows still launches through ComSpec (R-1034), and a refusal (R-1035) still spawns nothing. Eight rows: R-2020 and R-2022 to R-2027 in FEAT-013 SUB-013 after R-1036, R-2021 in FEAT-015 after R-952, with R-2023 and R-2024 also applying to FEAT-015. CAP-04 moves from 443 to 451 rows, FEAT-013 from 165 to 172 and FEAT-015 from 113 to 114. Tests: the new `pi-launch-limits.test.mjs`, nine checks on a sh-wrapped (or `pi.cmd`) fake pi that starts its own child node, with a 3 s limit. The setup README gains one Idempotence sentence and a tests-table row.

**Evidence.** CI run 39384200809 on draft pull request #107 at 4d04b56e (GitHub's merge commit 8c297be0 merges 4d04b56e into its own ancestor 385c633f, so the tree tested is 4d04b56e's): macOS 176 PASS, 0 FAIL, 2 SKIP of 178 files (7,848 checks pass); Ubuntu 175 PASS, 0 FAIL, 3 SKIP (7,787); Windows 161 PASS, 0 FAIL, 17 SKIP (6,783 pass, 106 skip), its skips main's declared ones; install-check passes on macOS and Windows. On native Windows pi-launch-limits prints 9 PASS and 2 SKIP lines. The SKIPs are R-2026 and R-2027's SIGINT check, which also print PASS after skipping, so seven checks ran there. R-2023 is among them: at all four stops the taskkill tree kill ended cmd.exe, pi's node and pi's child. Build 1's CI (run 39379023422 at 4dcc19b5) also read 0 failing on all three legs. The seat's wrong-code pairs on macOS: build 1 went 23 of 24 red, and B3 survived, since the tests could not tell a stop at the limit from the backstop's 5 s later (record `seat-mutate-output-4c67ba2c.txt`, commit 98a81ca7). Build 2 went 27 of 29 red (record `seat-mutate-output-4d04b56.txt`, commit cee89671): B3 is red, the new S1 to S3 are red, and S4 (a second signal during the grace is ignored) and S5 (a child that closes during the grace is reported as an ordinary result) survive, declared, since no check sends two signals or reads the relay's result after a signal. The pairs ran on macOS only; the Windows-only taskkill and verbatim-argument pairs did not run. The independent check ran on build 1, 4c67ba2c, and HOLDS over 11 probes with no MUST and two known bugs. A hung fake pi stopped the CLI dry run and doctor at 30 s with no process left; real pi 1.0.2 gave main's rows, each launch about 30 ms slower; forced win32 kept the ComSpec command line intact. Build 2 fixed its known bug 1 (R-2027). The trace reads 1,551 rows, 0 off form; map:check reads 339 modules, 0 problems. The seat's record is `docs/reviews/pi-probe-timeout-2026-10-20/seat-verify-4d04b56e.md`, with the Windows log and the independent check beside it.

**Plan and build.** The seat's plan went to one adversary, which amended it. R-2026 sends each of its three signals in its own run, since a relay without a SIGHUP handler left both fake processes alive after a group SIGHUP. The fake pi starts its own child node, and its sh wrapper ends with `exit $?`, so a shell that execs node cannot pass R-2023. The relay and pi drop `windowsHide`, inferred from libuv's source to take the launch off the owner's console, and the relay exits after it reports. The tree file joined the file list, R-2024 became a plain shall row, R-2022 builds its folder from `paths.mjs`'s `repoRoot`, and the arithmetic became 30 + 2 × 120 = 270 s. The simpler design, a detached spawnSync with a later group kill, works on macOS but fails on Windows, where cmd.exe is gone before taskkill can walk its tree, and Ctrl-C would no longer reach pi. A pi gpt-5.6-sol builder built it through pi-worker (two builds): 4c67ba2c, then 5389875b, which fixed the independent check's known bug 1 and the pair survivor B3 (the elapsed bound now sits below the backstop). Claude Opus 5.5 (the final reviewer) and Claude Fable 5.1 (the land reviewer) review it through review-ledger.

**Carried to HANDOFF.**

- pi-probe-timeout: new lines, one each, for the combined 1 MiB output line (the independent check's known bug 2); the EACCES wording; a pi that leaves a child holding its output reading as stopped at the limit; taskkill missing or denied on Windows; Windows Ctrl-C untested; killing nana-setup alone; a hung pi costing doctor two version limits; one more node process per launch; doctor's other probes unbounded; a pi that leaves its process group; and the pair survivors S4 and S5.

Its known bug 1, Ctrl-C during `pi install` SIGKILLing pi at once so pi's settings lock stayed behind (pi treats it as stale after about 10 s), is fixed by build 2: the relay passes the signal to pi's group and waits `RELAY_SIGNAL_GRACE_MS` (1 s) before the kill (R-2027). ## 2026-10-20 — both seats and doctor name a nana config file that does not parse, with its place and repair, never its text

Spend served the current priority's Windows line ("on macOS and Windows, installation and every hook included") through the queue's Windows fixes: the objective that both seats print at session start, and the Windows checklist's objective step. HANDOFF carried readme-windows-checklist's review note: step 7 sets `objective.path` in `nana-pack.json`, says nothing about backslashes in JSON, and so a pasted Windows path gives a parse error. The plan's probe on main 2cd533d9 with a temp home showed what followed. The Claude Code hook printed the default `nana-objective.md` block with no notice, since `loadUserObjective` read an unparseable file as no blocks. pi printed the same block, and `loadConfig` set the gate stop, so every gated tool stopped. Doctor read `✗ pi nana-pack.json missing or unparseable: <path>`. V8 on Node 22.22.2 and 24.22.0 alike reports `Bad escaped character in JSON at position 49 (line 2 column 48)`; an unquoted path gives `Unexpected token 'C', …` with a slice of the file, so no new surface may show the parser's message.

**The change.** `lib/json-text.mjs` gains `jsonErrorPlace`, which reads only V8's trailing `(line L column C)` through the contract constant `JSON_ERROR_PLACE`, `jsonParseFailure`, which classifies a bad escaped character or bad control character error as `forward-slash` and every other parse error as `manual`, `configFailureDetail`, the one renderer, and `CONFIG_FAILURE_PREFIX` (`NANA-PACK CONFIG UNPARSEABLE: `). `lib/config.ts`'s `readConfigFile` records that classification from its one existing read, after the BOM strip; `loadConfig` and `loadUserObjective` add `configFailure` (file, place when known, repair kind) to the objective settings, so the hook and the extension are untouched and R-018's byte identity holds by construction. `lib/objective.ts` puts one line right after the heading: the prefix, the file, ` at line L, column C` when known, then "Write objective.path with forward slashes because JSON reads a single backslash as an escape." or "Repair the JSON by hand.", then "Tell the user before spending." It shows beside an UNAVAILABLE marker and in the internal-error block too. ## 2026-10-19 — doctor's last line names install only for the ✗ rows install would repair

Spend served the current priority's installation line, for both seats on macOS and Windows: doctor is the check a seat reads after install, and its last line sent every ✗ row to install. On a temp copy of main 531ff1ec (the plan's probes, macOS), runDoctor printed `<n> missing — run: nana-setup install` whatever the ✗ rows were. An `install --home` without pi-subagents read `1 missing — run: …`, though install never installs pi-subagents. A foreign folder at `skills/spec` plus two removed rules read `3 missing — run: …`, though install refuses spec. A settings.json of `{"hooks": {},}` read `34 missing — run: …`, though install aborts before any write. A forced-win32 real home printed the same beside ✗ `PATH resolves pi-review`, and install cannot put the bin folder on the Path. No test pinned the line.

**The change.** In `packages/nana-setup/bin/nana-setup.mjs`, runDoctor, only when some row is ✗, calls `refuseCwdRelativePiHome(layout, "this install")` and then `install(layout, { dryRun: true })`. A ✗ row is install's when a dry-run row labelled `row.installLabel ?? row.label` reads created or updated; every other ✗ row is a fix by hand. The last line takes one of four forms: all install's, byte-identical to main's line; none, `<n> missing — fix by hand as each ✗ line says: <labels>`; mixed, the same labels then `; then run: nana-setup install for the other <m>`; and a SetupError refusal, `<n> missing — nana-setup install will not run until this is fixed: <first refusal line>`. Labels print once each, in row order, and every form keeps main's ` (and see the <w> ! above)` suffix. Build 2 added a fifth: any other dry-run error prints `could not predict nana-setup install repairs (<code>) — <n> missing — run: nana-setup install`, after every row, with exit 1 and no stack. In `lib/doctor.mjs`, diagnose's `add` takes an optional install label, stored only when given; three rows pass one, because install names them differently: the private rule, the shared memory index and the pi objective file. Rows with no install step (the node floor, pi executable, pi-subagents, mcp.json, the project file, PATH resolves pi-review, pi package source, the desk service) are by hand by construction. The `all good` line, the `!`-only line, every row and every exit code stay as they were. The setup README gains one paragraph and a tests-table row. The new `tests/doctor-fix-line.test.mjs` holds eight checks, R-1990 to R-1997, which sit in FEAT-015 after R-1766; CAP-04 moves from 416 to 424 rows and FEAT-015 from 96 to 104.

## 2026-10-19 — the review tools' tests wait for a reviewer's whole launch record

Spend served the current priority's Windows line through CI's Windows leg, which blocks release, and through the macOS suite every land runs. The review tools' tests failed in both with no real defect. immutable-review's fake reviewer wrote its launch record in two steps, the header and then the argv, and the test took the file's existence as a whole record: on a loaded Mac at install-pins' land it read the header alone, and two checks failed with `observed prompt text empty` and `standardOccurrences 0`. Every watched wait was a fixed 5 s: Windows run 39348142806 failed reclaim with `killedCheckout ""`, because the killed review had not started its reviewer in time. In the same run the final `rmSync` threw an uncaught EBUSY on the test's temporary folder, and the runner's FAIL-only excerpt never showed it. review-ledger's signal section waited the same 5 s, then read the pid file whole; a read between the file's creation and its write gives pid 0, and `process.kill(0, 0)` always succeeds.

**The change.** Tests only. A new helper, `packages/nana-pack/tests/launch-wait.mjs`, exports `awaitLaunchRecord(file, { closed, isComplete, limitMs, pollMs })` and two chosen tunables: `LAUNCH_RECORD_WAIT_MS` 60 s (twelve times the old wait, above the slowest whole check seen, 34.7 s on Windows) and `LAUNCH_RECORD_POLL_MS` 25 ms. It reads first, returns the text once the caller's completeness test holds, and returns null only after the launcher has closed or the limit has passed. immutable-review now runs one Node fake body on every platform, through a sh wrapper that execs it on POSIX so pi-review's pid stays; the body writes the pid file, then the whole record to `<OBSERVE>.part` in one write, and renames it onto OBSERVE. Its dirty-state, signal and reclaim launches wait through the helper with each launcher's close promise, and the signal check signals only a running launcher. The final `rmSync` retries 5 times 100 ms apart (both chosen), then prints one FAIL line, `the test's temporary folder is removed at the end`, with the error code and path. ## 2026-10-19 — the mutation runner's lock check passes on Windows, and a lock release gets its own five-minute limit

Spend served the current priority's Windows line through the queue's urgent-first item: CI's Windows leg blocks release, and main failed the mutation runner's lock contention check there in most runs. mutation-runner-win-prune (landed 32d6aa8b) added a cross-process worktree-operation lock; its contention check R-1776 runs 8 child workers for 300 acquisitions each and needs zero overlap, complete ownership and nothing left on disk. The seat's scratch run 39357872086 (draft PR #92, main d4423eff) failed it in 11 of 12 hosted Windows runs. It did not fail every run: hook-output-fail-open, install-dry-run-pi-packages, knowledge-unreadable-root and win-silent-skips each read 0 failing on Windows with the lock in their tree, and main's own CI run 39368683280 at 6bc2f727 failed it again. Build 1 followed the first brief's leading hypothesis, a release that meets Windows' delete-pending EPERM and gives up at the 30 s acquisition limit, leaving a live owner's lock behind; it made release retry with no limit. The scratch run 39364310814 at 0ad43c1d still failed 10 of 12. The seat decoded the ten failure records (table in `build-brief-2.md`): every failing run had workers SIGKILLed by the test's own 30 s per-child timer, 2 to 8 of 8 per run; every recorded overlap came in a run with kills, almost all from the highest-numbered workers, the last spawned and so the last killed; the lock and marker left on disk follow from the kills. The 12 runs reached 1,927 to 2,350 of 2,400 acquisitions in 30 s, so the timer killed workers mid-section, and a surviving worker then took over the dead pid's lock, found its marker and recorded an "overlap". That reading is the seat's, inferred from the records; build 2's passing runs fit it.

**The change.** In the test, for R-1776 only: the contention block gets `CONTENTION_BUDGET_MS` = 120 s, defined once with its measured provenance (four times the 30 s window the 12 runs measured). At the budget the test writes a stop file each worker checks between acquisitions, never inside the critical section, waits `CONTENTION_STOP_GRACE_MS` (5 s, chosen), then SIGKILLs only the workers still running; the per-child safety timer becomes budget + grace + 5 s. The failure record gains `timedOut` and `killedWorkers`, a timed-out run fails as a timeout, and its overlaps print marked as recorded after a kill, not as a lock failure. The strength is unchanged: 8 workers, 2,400 acquisitions, zero overlap, complete ownership, the observer. In the product: `withWorktreeOperationLock`'s release no longer stops at the 30 s acquisition limit, which left a live owner's lock behind for every waiter. It retries until the lock is gone or the new sealed `WORKTREE_LOCK_RELEASE_WAIT_LIMIT_MS` passes (300,000 ms in `mutation-runner-config.mjs`; chosen: ten acquisition windows for Windows' delete-pending state, still bounded), then reports one line naming the lock and the limit and throws. New row R-1960 pins both halves through the lock's injection hooks: a release that meets EPERM past the acquisition limit still releases, and a child whose release always fails stops at an injected limit with one report and an error, its lock left. R-1778 now covers acquisition only, and its check drops the release half; the sealed-values check pins the new limit. CAP-07 moves from 300 to 301 rows and FEAT-031 from 85 to 86.

## 2026-10-19 — on Windows, pi-review and pi-worker no longer stop a busy pi as stalled under a decimal-comma format

Spend served the current priority's Windows line for both seats: pi-review and pi-worker run every review and every build in either seat, and HANDOFF's queue puts the Windows fixes first. On Windows the watchdog read pi's CPU time as `(Get-Process -Id N).CPU`, a double that Windows PowerShell prints with the user's decimal mark. Under a decimal-comma format such as German, `Number("0,6416708")` is NaN, which the watchdog turned into 0. Every poll then read `cpu=0s`, the CPU looked flat, and the watchdog stopped a busy pi as stalled: every review and build on such a machine. The seat's probe P1 confirmed it on a hosted Windows runner (scratch run 39355882657, main 27fb9d3c's code, an en-US runner): Windows PowerShell 5.1.26100 printed `1,5` and the CPU value `0,90625` under an in-process de-DE thread culture; after `Set-Culture de-DE`, a new PowerShell printed CPU `0,5`; and main's win32-launch check `Windows: a busy pi is not stopped as stalled` failed, with `cpu=0s` lines and STALL. Two smaller faults sat beside it on every system. A failed read returned 0 and main's ps parse turned `n/a` into NaN, so a broken reader read either as a flat zero or as never flat. And a pi that exited during a read could end as STALL when the read repeated the last time, which the plan's adversary reproduced; Linux keeps an exited child's time until its parent reaps it.

**The change.** `pi-watchdog.mjs` exports `parseCpuSample(raw, platform)`, which returns seconds or null: on win32 a trimmed whole count of 100-nanosecond ticks divided by the new sealed `WIN_CPU_TICKS_PER_SECOND` (10,000,000 in `worker-config.mjs`, its contract .NET's TimeSpan.TicksPerSecond); elsewhere a trimmed ps time `[dd-][hh:]mm:ss[.fraction]`; any other text null. The win32 read now runs `(Get-Process -Id N).TotalProcessorTime.Ticks`, an Int64 that prints as digits in every format; both reads stay `execSync` by name through the shell, and a thrown read gives null. After each read the poll loop yields once with setImmediate; if pi has exited, the attempt ends by pi's own exit with no cpu line. Otherwise a null sample prints `cpu=unreadable flat=n/m`, counts as flat and keeps the last readable time. The plan ruled that an unreadable sample counts as flat: "no sample" would let a dead reader switch stall detection off, and pi-review has no wall-clock ceiling. The pack README's review-runner paragraph says both in two sentences. The new `watchdog-cpu.test.mjs` holds the five checks: R-1890 (Windows only) wraps the real Windows PowerShell 5.1 in a `powershell.cmd` that sets a de-DE thread culture, proves the wrapper prints `1,5` for `[double]1.5`, and needs a busy pi to print four cpu lines, each with positive seconds, then exit 0 with no STALL; R-1891 and its seal pin the parser; R-1892 cycles a fake reader through good, `n/a`, good and failing reads; R-1893 releases pi during a read that then fails or repeats the last time. The fold, in the immutable-review test only: its stall check's fake pi lives a chosen 180 s and its guard waits a chosen 120 s, both 30 s before, since run 39348142806's Windows leg printed one cpu line in 30 s. Rows R-1890 to R-1893 sit in FEAT-007's SUB-008 after R-1395, shared with FEAT-006; CAP-02 moves from 180 to 184 rows, FEAT-007 from 121 to 125 and SUB-008 from 34 to 38.

**Evidence.** CI run 39362479464 on draft pull request #93 at 3e998bf2 (GitHub's merge commit 4b859b60 merges 3e998bf2 into its own ancestor 8a9ff9a3, so the tree tested is 3e998bf2's): macOS 167 PASS, 0 FAIL, 2 SKIP of 169 files (7,735 checks pass); Ubuntu the same file counts (7,680); Windows 151 PASS, 1 FAIL, 17 SKIP (6,675 pass, 1 fail), its skips main's declared ones; install-check passes on macOS and Windows. The one Windows failure is main's mutation runner lock check, which the urgent mutation-runner-win-lock lane fixes; this lane touches no mutation runner file. On that en-US runner watchdog-cpu passes 5 and printed `PASS R-1890: on Windows a busy pi runs to its exit when PowerShell writes a decimal comma`; win32-launch passes 15 and printed `PASS Windows: a busy pi is not stopped as stalled`; immutable-review passes 16 with 2 skips, the fold's stall check included. So the seat promotes R-1890: its test marker becomes a `req:` marker, and the row reads implemented with that CI run as evidence. Build 1's CI run 39358574887 failed R-1890 on its own precondition: on the en-US runner the control printed `1.5`, while the run itself rose from 1.44 to 6.11 s of CPU and succeeded with no STALL. Build 2 runs the control through cmd's shell, so its PATH lookup reaches the wrapper, as the product's own read already did. The seat's P1 re-run on build 1's tip under a de-DE user culture (scratch run 39358595464) passed win32-launch 15, the busy-pi check included, and watchdog-cpu 5; build 2 changed only the test file. R-1893 passed natively on all three Windows runs, so the adversary's next likeliest wrong claim, that one setImmediate yield sees a Windows exit, held there. Build 2 added `01:00:00` and `1-02:03:04`, and the re-run on 3e998bf2 went 18 of 18 red, each by exactly its named titles, 0 survived. No pair ran on Windows, so no run has shown R-1890 red on the old `.CPU` read; the Windows evidence is CI and the two P1 runs. The independent check ran on build 1, 62627846, on macOS only, and held over eleven probes with no MUST: the parser reads real ps output and refuses comma, point and empty Windows text; macOS ps prints a point under German and French locales; busy and idle fake pis succeed and stall with the real ps; a forced-on Windows tick read behind a fake `powershell` sends the tick expression and behaves the same; and a pi that exits during a real ps read ends by its own status. ## 2026-10-19 — on Windows, install repairs Claude Code hook settings carried from a Mac or Linux home

Spend served the current priority's installation-and-hooks line on Windows ("installation and every hook included"), through its queue line for the Windows fixes, the Windows install shape part. A settings.json copied or synced from a Mac or Linux home is the likeliest Windows starting point. The plan's probe on main 32d6aa8b, a temp clone, a temp home and forced win32: install printed `already wired` for the objective, adoption, shared-memory and roster notice hooks, though all four named a missing `<home>/.claude/hooks/…`; the `Bash` verifier stayed and install appended a second one under `Bash|PowerShell`; the first installer's unquoted knowledge entry, `NODE_NO_WARNINGS=1 node <path> hook`, also read `already wired`. Doctor then read ✗ on 5 settings rows, and a second install changed nothing. The causes, in `lib/settings.mjs`: win32 `installerTarget` had no shell form for the five Node hooks and no unquoted knowledge form, `mergeRepoHooks` scanned only the wanted matcher, and `hasHook` read the dead shell form as present. HANDOFF's stale-copies-hooks residual carried the doubled verifier.

## 2026-10-19 — the mutation runner removes a scratch worktree git refuses to remove, and its parts take turns at git

Spend served the current priority's queue line for the Windows fixes, its maintainer-tools part, and CI's Windows leg, which now blocks release. The shared mutation runner ended each scratch worktree with `git worktree remove --force`, ignored a failure and deleted the folder, so git kept the entry as "prunable". Windows CI run 39305895780 (win-pi-registration-test's first run) failed R-1231's three-shard cleanup check this way; the check had passed in 43 of 44 saved Windows runs. Cause, inferred by the plan: git refuses before it deletes anything, or fails on the entry's own files under `.git/worktrees/`, and another shard's git call reading them is the likely Windows trigger.

**The change.** Build 1 (4aaafdc1): one helper serves a shard's own end and the parent's dead-shard cleanup. The first remove is the old call by full path. On failure, up to `WORKTREE_REMOVE_RETRIES` (3) times, it stops when `git worktree list --porcelain` no longer lists the entry, waits `WORKTREE_REMOVE_RETRY_MS` (250 ms) synchronously, deletes the `wt` folder, and removes again by git's unique suffix `<scratch folder base name>/wt`. An entry still listed after the last retry gets one line, `seat-mutate: git worktree entry <wt> is still listed after 3 retries`: in the shard's part file, or in the parent's notes for a dead shard, so it reaches the output once and the record once. The runner never runs `git worktree prune`, which acts on every entry, and never passes `--force` twice, so a lock someone set stays and is named. The KEEP paths are unchanged. Build 2 (bd3df051): CI's Windows leg on build 1 failed R-1230's existing scratch check, because shard 2's `git worktree add` read shard 1's half-removed admin folder (`failed to read .git/worktrees/wt/commondir`). One operation lock, a file in the run's parts folder, now covers each worktree add and each whole removal with its retries; a waiter tries again every `WORKTREE_LOCK_WAIT_MS` (25 ms) and replaces a lock whose holder process is gone. Six rows in FEAT-031, R-1770 to R-1775, each with one check in `mutation-runner.test.mjs`; the fixture gains the `drop-dotgit` and `lock-self` probe modes, each with a `-selfkill` form, and T4 counts removes in a `GIT_TRACE` file. T1 passing on Windows means Git for Windows found the entry by its forward-slash suffix, which the plan's adversary had not tried there. Build 1's run 39330086149 (4aaafdc1) failed only that one Windows file, 30 pass and 1 fail. Per the builder's reports, each wrong-code try turned its named check red: no retry (T1, T2, T4, T5), every retry run whatever the listing (T4), `prune --expire now` (T3), one retry or no wait (T4), the dead-shard line to the console only (T5), the helper under KEEP (R-1231), a raw full-path list compare (T1); R-1775's check was red before build 2 and with the lock bypassed, and the test file passed three runs in a row. ## 2026-10-19 — the install check runs one real pi turn in a fresh install, on macOS and Windows

Spend served the current priority's installation line, for the pi seat: the priority names both seats, installation and every hook, on macOS and Windows. The install check proved install, pi registration, a pi RPC session and each Claude Code hook in a temporary home, but by its own README it did not invoke pi's prompt-time hooks. So a fresh install whose pi turn lost the objective, the rulings, the writing rule or the knowledge pull, or whose gate let the verifier sample through, still passed. The plan's stub run of main also gave PASS `pi session` for an `extension_error` line, an `objective unavailable:` notice and a roster-unavailable widget, and PASS `hook adoption` for a stale line and a stale-check-unavailable line.

**The change.** A new pi extension fixture, `packages/nana-setup/lib/install-check-turn.mjs` (six-tag header, default export), loads only through `-e` and sits in no pi package manifest (R-1796). It imports the faux provider from the ROOT `@earendil-works/pi-ai`, which pi aliases for every extension, and registers a sealed provider and model. Its first answer records the system prompt and the user messages, then calls bash with the verifier hit sample; its second records each tool result and writes the record as JSON into the temporary home. `install-check.mjs` runs the turn after `pi session` through `piRun`, so win32 goes through findPi and winCommand: from the fixture project, with the base environment (no `NANA_ROLE`, so the 2026-10-09 knowledge ruling holds), `--offline -e <fixture> --provider <p> --model <m> --no-session -p "<prompt> <token>"` and a sealed 60 s timeout. The exported pure judge `judgePiTurn` fails `pi turn` on a non-zero exit (naming the last stderr line), a missing record, an `Extension error (` stderr line, a stale or stale-check-unavailable line in the system prompt, or a system prompt missing the run token, `## Standing rulings (nana)` or `<nana-writing>`. It also fails when no user message starts with `[nana:knowledge]` and names the note file, or no errored bash result starts with `nana-gate: verifier pipe blocked (headless fail-closed):`. The pi session's spawn keeps 100,000 characters of output, and the exported reader `readPiSessionEvents` fails the line on an `extension_error` event or an extension notice, widget or status holding "unavailable" in any letter case, skipping non-JSON lines. The `hook adoption` line also fails on a line that starts with either stale prefix, imported from `stale-copies-config.mjs`. `PI_TURN`, `PI_SESSION` and `SPAWN_TIMEOUT_MS.turn` are sealed with provenance, and the note's file name has one sealed name. ## 2026-10-19 — pi-review and pi-worker end an attempt as soon as pi exits

Spend served the current priority's review and builder launchers, which both seats run on macOS and Windows. pi-watchdog, behind pi-review and pi-worker, noticed pi's exit only at its next poll (15 s by default), so every attempt ended up to a poll late and a run of instant failures waited a full poll each. Worse, a pi killed by a signal the watchdog did not send (SIGKILL, or the SIGABRT Node raises when it runs out of memory) hung the after-loop wait on a `close` event that had already fired. pi-review then exited 13 ("unsettled top-level await") without retrying and left its review checkout and reservation for the next launch to reclaim. pi-worker `--lane` left `nana-lane.lock` with the dead pid, and the next lane run in that worktree was refused; nothing reclaimed that lock.

One `ended` promise per attempt settles on pi's `exit` or `error` event; each poll races its timer, the signal wait and `ended`, then clears the timer, so pi-review does not live out the poll; the after-loop wait is `await ended`. The checks after a wake keep their order, and stall, ceiling, signal handling and retries are unchanged. The pack README's watchdog paragraph gains one sentence. Six new rows, R-1390 to R-1395, each with one check in the new `watchdog-exit.test.mjs`.

**Evidence.** The plan's probes, main against the fix: pi-review closed 4,854 ms after pi exited at `--poll 5` against 155 ms; three instant failures took 6,048 ms against 130 ms; an exit between polls ended the attempt 3,968 ms later against 6 ms. The seat's eight wrong-code pairs all turn their checks red, 0 survived. The independent check holds with no MUST; its one known bug (a background child's output written after pi exits is no longer captured) is a carried residual, and the Windows leg verified its other residual (the signal checks on Windows). On Windows immutable-review took 27.9 s against about 78 s on other runs; the fix is the likely cause (inferred).

**Plan and build.** The seat's plan and one adversary, who amended it: a sixth check for the lane lock, WE1 timed from pi's own exit, and a sixth wrong-code pair that only the between-polls check catches. Claude Sonnet 5 built it in one pass. Opus reviews as the final reviewer and Fable as the land reviewer, under the power-mode lineup.

The install test did not pin the plain `node` form, and one Windows check passed with its behaviour removed. Build 3 fixed all seven. Run 3 passed all five files, the skipped sections ran natively and passed, and CI's Windows failing count fell from 38 of 150 files to 33. One reviewer.

## 2026-10-18 — the pi seat's handoff, display and post-edit tests on Windows

Spend served the current priority's pi seat on Windows: the handoff store and artifact, the staleness pointer, the trust checks, the display surfaces, the post-edit queue and the frontier checker. Their seven test files failed on Windows, and two of them stopped before their end.

**The change.** Tests only, no new row. Journal lines are parsed as JSON before their paths are compared, since JSON escapes each Windows backslash. Expected paths use the platform separator, and the expected pointer uses `~\` where Windows writes it; pi's own resolver expands that form. Temp homes are resolved to their long names, because Windows hands out short 8.3 names and the product will not shorten a path holding `~`. The post-edit queue's log path travels through an environment variable, not script source. Hostile names NTFS refuses use a Unicode line separator and a bidi override instead. The long-home block, the tab, CR and LF names and the POSIX lock-out cases skip on Windows, each with its reason.

**Plan and build.** Claude Sonnet 5 built it in four passes against CI's Windows leg on a draft pull request. Run 1: four of seven files passed. Brief 2 blamed the display test's `\\?\` prefix on its temp home, and run 2 proved that wrong. Build 3 found the source: `fs.mkdirSync` with `recursive` returns the first folder it made, and on Windows that path comes back in the `\\?\C:\` form, which cmd.exe refuses as a working folder. Run 3 left one check, whose expected JSON locator did not escape backslashes. Run 4 passed all seven files. The reviewer then sent the lane back once: the store test skipped its dangling-link cases on Windows as "POSIX symlinks", but Windows has symlinks. Build 5 runs them there, and run 5 passed all ten. CI's Windows failing count fell from 49 of 150 files to 38. One reviewer.

## 2026-10-17 — the pi seat's gate tests on Windows

Spend served the current priority's pi seat on Windows: the command gate, its policy paths, the lane write guard and the agent-folder resolution. Their five test files failed on Windows, two of them before their first check.

**The change.** Tests only, no new row: `USERPROFILE` set beside a moved `HOME`; file URLs turned into paths with `fileURLToPath` and paths into import URLs with `pathToFileURL`; the temp root standing in for `/tmp` on Windows; the live-working-folder case and the frozen desk's leg skipped on Windows with their reasons; the desk's pi resolver called lazily so the pack and nana-setup legs run.

**Plan and build.** Claude Sonnet 5 built it in three passes. Windows run 1: four of five files passed; the parity test died in its last cleanup with EBUSY. A retry did not help (run 2). Build 3 found the holder: the test had moved its own working folder into its temp home and never moved back, and Windows will not remove a process's working folder. Run 3 passed all five files. One reviewer.

**Lessons.** (1) An EBUSY that survives retries is a live holder, not a slow release; look for the process's own working folder first. (2) A test that changes its working folder must restore it before cleaning up.
## 2026-10-17 — both seats' session start on Windows

Spend served the current priority's "every hook working" on Windows: the objective and current priority each seat shows at session start, and the Claude Code seat's adoption line.

**The change.** One must-meet test, R-1340: on Windows, the installed objective and adoption SessionStart commands, run exactly as settings.json holds them in a fixture project with an objective and a priority, print the objective block naming that priority and the adoption line. The rest is test portability: `USERPROFILE` set beside `HOME` (Windows reads it), a relative path kept on one drive, Windows-legal hostile names in place of names NTFS refuses, and POSIX-only cases (named pipes, file ownership, file modes) skipped on Windows with their reasons.

**Plan and build.** Claude Sonnet 5 built it in three passes. The first Windows run showed the new check passing and the objective test running to its end (983 of 993; it had crashed at 94). Build 2 settled the named-pipe and ownership cases; the four path-display checks still failed, and the log printed no detail because the branch predated the verbose Windows leg. The seat merged main, which brought the verbose leg; build 3 found that the block's quoting doubles each backslash of a hostile path and derived the expectation from the product's own display function. The third run passed every target file; the Windows failing count fell from 56 to 50 of 150 files. One reviewer.

**Lessons.** (1) Merge the verbose CI leg into a Windows lane before its second round; a FAIL line with no detail costs a round. (2) Build the expected text with the product's own escaping, not by hand.

## 2026-10-17 — project files on Windows

Spend served the current priority's Windows fixes (Owner moved them up on 2026-10-17); this is the first of the Windows plan's lanes.

**The change.** `CLAUDE.md` is a regular one-line file, `@AGENTS.md`, on every system: Claude Code imports a repo-relative `@path` with no prompt. nana-pi's own `CLAUDE.md` changes from a symbolic link to that file; git for Windows had checked the link out as a 9-byte text file reading `AGENTS.md`, so Claude Code on the owner's Windows clone loaded no project instructions. `nana-setup project` writes the import file for a new project, `--check` accepts it or an existing link and flags the 9-byte file, and a refresh replaces that file and never writes through a link. The AGENTS.md working-region refresh closes its handle before the rename and retries a refused rename briefly, and it compares file identity with 64-bit stats. CI's Windows suite run is verbose. Rows R-1310 to R-1313.

**Plan and build.** Claude Sonnet 5 built it in five passes, each driven by one Windows CI run on a draft pull request. Run 1: the refresh passed on Windows; the project test crashed on a bare `npm` spawn. Run 2: a raw path handed to `import()`. Run 3: 112 of 121, eight of them line-ending failures, which the line-endings lane then fixed, and one test that hard-coded a forward slash. Run 4: the project test passed 121 of 121, and the owner-swap check showed the refresh overwriting a file its owner had replaced: Windows file IDs are 64-bit, and as JavaScript numbers two different files can compare equal. Build 5 compares them as 64-bit integers; run 5 and a rerun of its Windows job passed every target. sol's final round then found one more data-loss case: the rename retry did not re-check `AGENTS.md`, so an editor's save between two attempts would be overwritten. Build 6 re-checks identity and bytes before every retry, with a test that injects one refused rename while the owner rewrites the file. Round 2 found the re-check ran before the 20 ms delay; build 7 moved the delay first, so the re-check runs just before each retry's rename. A save in the instant between that re-check and the rename can still be overwritten: Windows has no atomic compare-and-replace, so it is a known limit.

**Lessons.** (1) Verbose CI output paid for itself on its first run: every round after it named its cause. (2) An intermittent Windows check is a bug report, not noise: runs 1 and 3 passed, runs 2 and 4 failed, and the cause was a data-loss guard that silently did not work there. (3) Fix the shared cause first: the line-endings lane cleared eight of this lane's failures.

Spend served the current priority's "every hook working" on Windows. Since 2026-10-12 the seat's hooks run on Windows from the checkout, but the only Windows proof was that each exits 0 with no module error; the Windows plan's adversary pointed out that a hook printing nothing would pass that.

**The change.** One must-meet test, R-1330: on Windows, the installed knowledge hook command, run exactly as settings.json holds it with a prompt that matches a fixture store, prints a pull block naming the fixture file. The rest is test portability, each skip printing its reason: file URLs passed to node as paths, separator-neutral comparisons, a Windows-legal hostile file name, the win32 exec-form hook entries instead of `~/.claude/hooks` links, POSIX-only mode bits, and a working folder Windows cannot delete.

**Plan and build.** Claude Sonnet 5 built it in two passes. CI's first Windows run on the draft pull request showed the knowledge pull working on Windows and the knowledge hook test running to its end, the 16-process index-lock race included; two checks failed on Windows path spellings (a backslash before `n` read as JSON's newline, and two spellings of one path). The second run passed all seven target files; the Windows failing count fell from 62 to 56 of 150. One reviewer.

(2) The seat's brief told the builder to keep the new row `planned` until Windows proved it; the trace rail fails a planned row that a test traces, so a row flips when its test is written, and the Windows run is the evidence.

## 2026-10-17 — Windows line endings

Spend served the current priority's Windows test fixes, which the owner moved up on 2026-10-17. Git for Windows' default `core.autocrlf=true` and a `.gitattributes` with no line-ending rule gave every Windows checkout of nana-pi, and copier's clone of it, CRLF text files; the TypeScript template's scripts split lines on `\n` only, and seven test files failed on CI's Windows run, two of them by crashing.

**The change.** `.gitattributes` gains `* text=auto eol=lf`. The TypeScript template's code-map, readme-check and trace scripts split on `\r?\n`. The mutation runner creates and resets its scratch worktrees with `core.autocrlf=false`. Rows R-1320 to R-1322: a clone made with autocrlf on checks out LF; both templates' checks pass on a rendered project rewritten to CRLF; a scratch worktree from a repository with autocrlf on holds the committed bytes.

**Plan and build.** The Windows plan (`docs/reviews/windows-fixes-2026-10-17/`: six readers classified the 48 failing files in scope, an agent cut nine lanes, an adversary attacked them) made this its second lane. Claude Sonnet 5 built it in one pass and rehearsed it on the Mac in a clone made with autocrlf on (407 checks, none failing). CI's first Windows run on the lane passed all eight target files; the Windows failing count fell from 69 of 149 files to 62. One reviewer, under the feature-first bar.

**Lessons.** (1) A Windows line-ending bug reproduces on a Mac: clone with `-c core.autocrlf=true`. That rehearsal turned an eleven-minute CI round into a local run. (2) One line of repository configuration fixed more than any test edit could; look for the shared cause before the per-file one.

## 2026-10-17 — the runtime map

Spend served the owner's 2026-10-16 request to build code runtime evaluation into the code map: per test file, the repository code it actually runs, children included, and how long it takes, kept outside the repository and never read by the map check.

**The change.** With `NANA_COVERAGE_DIR` set, the suite runner gives each test file its own V8 coverage folder and writes a record of its path, label and seconds, then a completion record; unset, it behaves as before. `npm run map:measure` (`scripts/runtime-measure.mjs`) runs the locked suite with that knob (the lock runner starts the suite in its own process group), credits each test file with the tracked files its process and its node children ran, and writes the data under the clone's git common directory, so a linked worktree and the main checkout share it. A run that ends without its completion record, or with a count that differs, keeps the earlier data and exits non-zero; a stop ends the suite's whole tree, removes the coverage folder and leaves the caller alone. `npm run map:impact <file>` prints the generator's output unchanged, then the measured tests for each file, longest first, with seconds and any FAIL label, marks the whole section stale when tracked files changed, and prints one note when there is no data. Rows R-1270 to R-1278.

**Plan and build.** The plan had 30 rows, 32 checks and 71 wrong-code pairs after two sol plan rounds. Under the owner's 2026-10-17 feature-first ruling the seat cut it to nine must-meet tests; one adversary added three of them (the real measurement from a linked worktree with no override, a stop sent twice, the zero line's note). Claude Sonnet 5 built it in one pass. The lane's independent check on the runner edit found that a runner check failed under the measurement's own coverage variable, so every real measurement ended red; the seat's real measurement confirmed it, and build 2 fixed the test. The seat's four wrong-code pairs on the runner edit all turned red, and the real measurement on build 2's tip passed 147 of 149 files (2 skipped) in about 13 minutes. In the final round astra said land; sol sent back three points under the new bar: two must-meet tests still passed with their feature removed (the recorded labels and seconds; the impact command's default data path), and an unstaged deletion of a tracked file crashed the impact view. Build 3 fixed all three. The seat then found that the new deletion test deleted and rewrote the checkout's own `.gitignore`; build 4 moved it into a fixture repository. The lane merged main after the rule lane landed, and one confirmation round covers the fixes and the merge.

**Lessons.** (1) A real run of the feature on the real repo found the one bug that blocked it; the fixture tests could not, because the fixture never ran under coverage. Keep the seat's real run in every lane whose feature runs the suite. (2) The cut held, and the new floor earned its keep: nine tests and four pairs covered what 32 checks and 71 pairs were written for, and the one round of send-backs was two must-meet tests that passed with their feature removed — the case the new standard makes blocking. (3) A test that needs a missing tracked file must build its own repository; deleting and restoring the checkout's file is never safe.
## 2026-10-17 — the working rules say feature-first development

Spend served the owner's 2026-10-17 ruling: stop chasing bug-free lanes, build each feature to its must-meet tests, and review for bugs that block the feature.

**The change.** The review standard's MUST is now a must-meet test that is missing or still passes with the feature removed, a bug that stops the feature's main use on a named platform, or one of four harms: data lost or corrupted, a test, build step or seat script writing outside the lane worktree or the temp folder (a product command writing where its contract says, such as install into the home folder, is not this harm), a broken install or hook, or something main does today no longer working. Every other finding is a known bug, fixed when someone hits it. The shared working pattern gives an ordinary lane one final reviewer and no plan review round, and defines the install, hook and gate lanes that keep two reviewers, wrong-code pairs and an independent check. The coding standards and the requirements skill write one row per must-meet test, no wider than the test, and drop clause-by-clause pinning. The seat guide reruns the mutation runner only in install, hook and gate lanes. The builder rules write only the brief's must-meet tests, plus a seal test per new sealed tunable. The pack README's mutation runner line now says exit 0 means the run completed, as sol noted on the split runner. Rows R-1300 and R-1301, with R-1101, R-1108, R-1110, R-1127 and R-1140 reworded.

**Plan and build.** The seat drafted the new text verbatim with six must-meet checks; one adversary attacked it, and the seat took most of its points, most importantly the MUST for a missing or empty must-meet test, the bounded write harm and the lane-class definition. The small-lane builder stopped after five minutes with no commit; Claude Sonnet 5 finished from its edits in one pass. The seat ran the suite and the install check; one reviewer, sol, reviews it under the new bar.

**Lessons.** (1) A rule a builder must follow belongs where every builder reads it: a Claude Code builder never sees pi-worker's preamble, so the must-meet line also sits in the coding standards. (2) A softer bar needs one hard floor: without the MUST for a missing or empty must-meet test, nothing would check the tests the whole process rests on.

## 2026-10-17 — one shared mutation runner, and feature-first development

Spend served the owner's 2026-10-16 report that lanes ran slower than expected. Each lane copied the seat's mutation runner, and the five-way split lived only in the latest copy.

**The change.** `packages/nana-pack/lib/mutation-runner.mjs` is one shared runner; a lane's pair table imports it and passes its pairs and an optional config, which merges an allowed set of values over the defaults. The runner applies each pair's edits in a scratch worktree of the tip, splits the pairs round-robin across five shard processes started 4 s apart, and writes one record. It locks the record file, resolves the tip and hashes the table once and refuses a shard that sees either move, refuses edit and test paths that leave the worktree, and cleans the scratch worktree of a shard that dies. Rows R-1230 to R-1244.

**Plan and build.** The first plan had 40 rows, 49 checks and 98 pairs; the seat cut it to 15 rows before sol's one plan round, whose two MUSTs (two runs sharing a record file; shards seeing different tips) became rows R-1242 and R-1243. Claude Sonnet 5 built it in one pass: 26 checks, all green in 44 s. Ported to the shared runner, the roster-notice lane's 71-pair table gave the same verdict on every pair as its committed record, at one shard (6:17) and at five (2:33); the seat ran it again at five. The suite passed on the build tip (146 of 148 files, 2 skipped, 12 minutes).

**Feature-first development.** While the build ran, the owner ruled that nana moves to feature-first development (the HANDOFF's Next list states it). Under his ruling the seat skipped this lane's own 43-pair run (the table is committed and all 43 pairs apply) and sent the lane to one final reviewer under the new bar. The runtime map's plan of 30 rows, 32 checks and 71 pairs is cut to seven must-meet tests.

**Lessons.** (1) The seat's own checking, not the reviewers, made lanes slow: the regroup lane took seven builds, and its three independent checks found 45, 52 and 47 issues, mostly tests that missed a clause. (2) A plan written row by row grows to match the tool's every edge; writing the must-meet tests first keeps it to the feature.

## 2026-10-17 — the seat works in parallel by default

Spend served the owner's 2026-10-16 request, after the lanes ran slower than expected, that the seat consider parallel work by default. The owner then chose one rule in the seat guide and a new lane limit: two lanes building plus one in planning.

**The change.** The seat guide gains two bullets and a new limit. Before ending its turn, the seat names and starts what waits on nothing else (another lane's build, a long mutation run in parts, separate research agents), while each lane's own steps stay in order. It runs the full suite whole, never splits a long run while a full suite runs on the same machine, and re-runs a check that fails on a time limit alone before calling it a failure. A lane in planning has no build yet. R-1140 is reworded and pinned by four new or renamed checks.

**Plan and build.** A planning workflow drafted it beside two other plans (a shared split runner, a runtime map). sol's one plan round sent it back: splitting runs while other work runs would cause false failures under load, so the rule now says when not to split. The small-lane builder copied the planned guide and test byte for byte in one pass; the plan's pair simulation catches 26 of 26 breaks.

**Lessons.** (1) A speed rule needs its own safety line: parallel work raises load, and load makes time-limited tests fail.

## 2026-10-16 — the regroup check

Spend served the current priority and the owner's 2026-10-14 ruling that turning an existing repo into a feature tree is a core nana feature. The lift could apply a grouping with a proof, but nothing checked an agent's grouping before the owner saw it.

**The change.** `node "$HOME/nana-pi/scripts/requirements-regroup.mjs" --root <dir> --proposal <file> --out <page>` checks a proposal — a lift grouping plus a `regroup` record — and writes a short review page. The lift's own dry run must pass. Each line the lift reports needs one reason, each row one reviewer verdict (keep, move or share, each target with its own reason and one outcome: carried, refuted or asked), each share the proposal adds, drops or moves by a merge a share verdict, each purpose, outcome and reason one accept-or-reject verdict quoting its current text, each gap its evidence, and each row placed by text alone a reason. The page leads with the questions, a feature table and every node with its label and purpose as the lift will write them, then the reported lines, the move and share targets, rejected claims, text-placed rows and refuted items; the full row list is an appendix. A failing run removes an earlier page and touches nothing else. Rows R-1170 to R-1180, R-1184 and R-1187.

**Plan and build.** The plan took three sol rounds and four seat amendments: one for a trace-rail helper the builder had to export, one for shares once the shares lane landed first, one for a share a merge moves, and one for a share riding on a reused feature ID. sol's third-round point (a move refused and replaced by a share) was declined and recorded. Claude Sonnet 5 built it in seven passes. After builds 2 to 4 the seat ran an independent check: five or six checkers attacked in private copies and a separate checker re-ran every finding. Those checks found 45, 52 and 47 confirmed findings, most of them tests that did not pin what their rows claim. After every build the seat ran the full suite and its mutation runner. Build 5 was a closed list with no independent check. sol's first final review then found three gaps: a share riding on a reused feature ID, evidence reached through a link outside the root, and angle brackets hiding proposal text on the page. Build 6 fixed them under a fourth amendment. The seat's mutation runner: 216 of 217 breaks caught at e5d71c6, run in five parallel parts; the one survivor drops a check that build 6's link-aware check now duplicates.

**What went wrong.** The second builder died on a network error after its last commit; the seat ran its closing checks. The seat's own build brief 1 told the builder to read evidence the wrong way, which made every basketball-geek row look text-placed; brief 2 corrected it. Build 3 narrowed the gap test and opened a hole for a status written as a list; build 4 removed a copied status check and opened one for a padded status. Each check round found more unpinned parts of the two long page rows, so after four builds the seat stopped and recorded the rest as residuals.

**Lessons.** (1) A refusal test must read the check's own words from stderr; a row ID in the output pins nothing when the lift echoes it. (2) A row that enumerates a dozen page parts invites a new finding every round; pin each part when it is written, or write the row smaller. (3) Removing a duplicate check needs a test for every input the duplicate caught.

**Also.** The shares entry below said a share line after a table is refused; the lift keeps it. The owner's Windows check passed, but CI's Windows test run still fails 68 of 144 files, so the shares notes' "done is met" was wrong and is corrected in `HANDOFF.md`.

## 2026-10-16 — the lift carries shares; the Windows check passed

Spend served the current priority and the owner's 2026-10-10 ruling, "we should allow multiple features pointing to the same requirements": the lift refused every `Also applies:` line, so no grouping could keep or change a share, and nana-pi's own ledger carries 31.

**The change.** One reader decides what a share line is: the tree parser's first `Also applies:` line of a feature. The lift copies it byte-identical when nothing changes, regenerates it when a grouping merges or demotes features or declares `shares_added` or `shares_dropped`, and refuses every other `Also applies:` line — fenced, in the head or tail, under a kept section, a second in a span, or unterminated (the first share line after a table is kept and moved after `Status:`). The proof recounts each feature's shares from the input and the declarations alone, never from the grouping's result list, so an undeclared drop or add fails. The plan prints one line per added or dropped share. Rows R-1181 to R-1183; R-1167 reworded.

**Plan and build.** A draft and two fact-checks; the proof check's MUST — three readers that disagreed around a fence — became the one-reader rule. sol's single plan round said LAND; its two notes (empty declaration lists mean no change; repeated IDs refused directly) went into the build brief, and the seat reworded R-1181 to one "shall" with the meaning unchanged. Claude Sonnet 5 built it in two passes; the second fixed five tests that accepted another check's refusal. An independent check found no share lost, duplicated, retargeted or invented with exit 0. The seat's mutation runner: 36 of 36 code breaks caught.

**Also.** the owner ran the Windows check on 2026-10-16 and it passed, which meets the current priority's 2026-10-24 "done". He asked whether nana makes agentic work consistent from session to session; a cold-start study (six agents, no memory) found nana's files answer most orientation questions but none of his standing rulings, which live only in memory — so he ruled for a separate rulings file every seat reads at startup.

## 2026-10-15 — the lift: a flat requirements ledger into the tree, with a proof

Spend served the current priority and the owner's 2026-10-14 ruling: "Lift is the tool that enables better regroup, but this is a core feature for nana, understanding existing repo and turn into feature trees, then development really becomes feature oriented". Every existing nana project still had a flat ledger, and a hand sort has no proof.

**The change.** `node "$HOME/nana-pi/scripts/requirements-lift.mjs" --root <dir>` prints the planned tree with each heading's row count, the moves and a proof line, and writes nothing. With no grouping given, it builds the default for a flat ledger: each Part becomes a capability, each `##` a feature and each `###` a subgroup, in file order, labels kept and purposes "Not yet sorted:"; the general engineering sections take the reserved CAP-90, FEAT-900 and SUB-900 to SUB-904. A grouping file (`--mapping`, pinned to the ledger's text) applies any tree, flat input or not; `--emit-mapping` writes the default, or the identity grouping for a ledger that already has a tree, as the regroup's starting point. A separate proof module, which imports nothing from the lift, checks every row byte for byte with its own line ending, a count of every other non-blank line derived from the input alone, blank lines by position where a section keeps its layout, the row-ID multiset, placement (derived from the input alone for the default), the reserved nodes and a clean tree check. `--write` runs only when the proof passes, git is present with a commit, the ledger and grouping match HEAD in every worktree, and the bytes have not changed since the proof. `--verify <rev>` lets a reviewer prove a committed lift against its base, byte for byte. The requirements skill carries the flow for both seats: dry run, the owner's yes, then write. Ledgers with shares (`Also applies:` lines) are refused in every form until the regroup lane adds share support. Rows R-1162 to R-1169.

**Plan and build.** Three research reads (the tree code, six real flat ledgers on this Mac read from copies, the flow) and two fact-checks shaped the plan; they caught an ANSI byte that would have been silently rewritten, a git check that only saw its own worktree, a Windows path break, and a proof that skipped blank lines. sol's plan rounds sent it back twice — the proof did not derive placement from the input, then applied that to supplied groupings too — and said LAND on the third. The seat's checks were written first (110 build cases red on main, 136/136 on a scratch build) and hardened against six ways a wrong build could pass. Claude Sonnet 5 built it in six passes. The second fixed a Windows short-path bug CI found (17 of 28 lift tests red there, all green after). The next three answered the seat's independent checks: the proof first trusted the grouping for its line regions, so a grouping could delete an intro, an owner's section or a field-labelled body line with a clean proof, and `--verify` did not prove. Build 4 replaced region matching with a count of every non-blank input line derived from the input alone, and build 5 stopped a plain 4-column table from losing its header. The last independent check fuzzed about 2,400 lifts and regroups and found nothing lost, duplicated, changed or invented; the four real ledgers come out byte-identical. The final reviews' first round sent it back once more — `--verify` compared decoded text, the worktree scan skipped the grouping file and staged removals, and a tree-form share line could be dropped — and a seventh pass closed all three. The seat's mutation runner: 80 of 80 code breaks caught at the final build, none surviving.

**What went wrong.** The first builder started the full suite in the background and waited for a notice that never came; it sat dead for about nine and a half hours, unpushed, until the owner asked "Probe?". No probe was armed on builder subagents, against his July and August rulings. Since then every builder and every long run gets a failure watcher and a liveness heartbeat, and builders run only their touched test files while the seat runs the suite and CI.

**Lessons.** (1) A builder that waits on its own background job can strand itself; arm a heartbeat at launch and keep long steps with the seat. (2) Compare canonical paths before relating them on Windows: an 8.3 short name and git's long name climb out of the repository. (3) A proof that takes its regions from the thing it checks leaks one case at a time; derive what must survive from the input alone. (4) A test that asserts only "refused" pins nothing when several checks overlap; assert each check's own message.

## 2026-10-13 — CI pins pi's dependency tree; the owner's review materiality ruling

Spend served the current priority: CI is how both platforms prove the install and hooks work, and from 2026-10-12 23:00Z every CI suite leg was red for an upstream reason.

**The break.** `@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent` 1.0.2 accepts any 1.x of its six sibling packages. `pi-codemode` 1.2.0, published 2026-10-12T23:00:01.855Z, removed two exports that pi 1.0.2's codemode tool imports. A fresh `npm i -g` of pi 1.0.2 therefore resolved the new codemode. `pi --version` and an RPC session still worked, because the bundled CLI inlines codemode; what broke was any code that imports pi's module graph. On CI's blocking macOS leg 18 test files failed (13 desk, 5 pack), on main too; Ubuntu went from 1 to 19 failing files and Windows from 67 to 69. This Mac kept its 10-04 install and was unaffected.

**The fix.** CI's two pi install lines now end with npm's `--before`, set to `PI_BEFORE: "2026-10-04T06:57:57Z"`, declared once beside `PI_VERSION` with its provenance: the seat's own pi 1.0.2 install moment, which reproduces this Mac's whole `npm ls -g --all` tree. Rows R-1090 to R-1092 pin it: every install line carries the flag (versioned or not), the value is declared once and sealed, and nothing sets npm's `before` through the environment or a root `.npmrc`, which would freeze `npm test` and pi's own installs too.

**Plan and build.** A planning workflow ran three researchers (npm's `--before` semantics, failure attribution per leg, the repo surface), a drafter and two adversarial fact-checkers; their corrections (the install log's package count cannot prove the pin; the cutoff window; an unversioned install line escaping the check) went in before sol's one plan round (92/100, four small fixes). The seat's acceptance script installs CI's own line into a scratch prefix, checks all eight `@earendil-works` packages at 1.0.2, imports pi, and runs the 18 drift files against it, with an unpinned control that must reproduce the break: 23 of 33 failed at launch, 33 of 33 on a prototype. luna built it in one 31-minute session; the seat re-ran the acceptance (33/33) and the ten planned code breaks (10/10 caught). CI run 38399666350: macOS 0 failing files, Ubuntu 1 (the known symlink check), Windows 67.

**The owner's review ruling.** Asked whether reviews could stop chasing edge cases, the owner got the numbers from the Claude Code hooks lane: five final rounds and 16 blocking findings, of which the seat judged 4 material, all in round 1; rounds 2 to 5 (about three and a half hours) chased contrived PowerShell inputs, citations and a stale number in the seat's notes. The rule from now: a blocking finding names a realistic input and a consequence that matters; everything else is a residual; no blocking finding means LAND (the land helper only accepts LAND, so "land with fixes" always cost a round); a confirmation round reviews only the delta.

**Lessons.** (1) Pin what CI installs to what the developer machine runs; a caret range on a fresh global install is a moving target. (2) Prove a pin by the resolved versions and the tests it un-breaks, not by a package count. (3) A planning workflow with adversarial fact-checks caught five wrong claims before the one plan round.

## 2026-10-12 — the Claude Code seat's hooks on Windows

Spend served the current priority: the owner's Windows machine runs Claude Code as a seat, and on Windows nana wired only the knowledge pull. The objective, adoption, shared-memory and verifier hooks were missing there.

**The change.** On Windows, install writes all five Claude Code hooks in exec form: `"command": "node"` and `"args"` holding the script's absolute path in the checkout, with no shell to parse the line. Claude Code documents this form from 2.1.139. The verifier's matcher is `Bash|PowerShell`, and the pipe guard now lexes PowerShell quoting for the PowerShell tool (backtick escapes, doubled quotes, here-strings, block comments, `$( … )` inside double quotes). Doctor checks each of the five entries and that its target resolves inside the checkout, runs the Node 22.18 floor check it used to skip, and prints the Claude Code floor as a note. An existing Windows knowledge entry moves to exec form in place, never twinned. macOS and Linux output is byte-identical to main.

**Plan.** Seat planning workflow (research, draft, two fact-checks), then three sol plan rounds: 70, 86, then LAND 100. Round 1 added the PowerShell lexer and split the spawn evidence into start, SessionStart output and verifier output; round 2 required every lexer case to carry a live `git commit`.

**Build — the owner's measurement lane, built by Claude Sonnet 5.5.** Build 1 was one session of 3 h 20 min (about 905k tokens, 466 tool calls). It passed the seat's 59 acceptance cases and the test-title check, and the real Windows CI leg found three checks that did not understand exec form, which it fixed. The seat's code-break runner then turned the plan's 24 breaks into 29 and caught 28. Explaining the weak one found a regression: the new merge step had dropped main's status-message check, so on macOS and Linux a hand-edited knowledge hook with a stale path was rewritten where main leaves it alone. Build 2 restored the check for a different message and pinned the one surviving break. Build 3 made a missing message count as different too. That first needed the seat's own acceptance seed fixed: it planted a stale entry with no status message, which the installer has never written. After build 3: 31 of 31 breaks caught, re-run by the seat; 59 of 59 acceptance cases; no test lost.

**Final reviews, round 1.** sol (6/10) and astra (78/100) both sent it back. The PowerShell lexer could hide a live commit two ways: a `#` inside a word such as `issue#123` or a URL fragment started a comment, and a `)` inside a comment closed a `$( … )` early. The merge still scanned only matcher-less groups, a second kept behaviour the planned breaks missed. Exec-form ownership went by file name, so a hand-written `C:/custom/nana-objective.mjs` would have been repaired to nana's checkout. Several rows claimed more than their tests pinned: a 5 s limit tested with 10 s, "exactly one JSON line" checked on the first line only. Build 4 fixed all of it: a `#` starts a comment only at a token boundary (PowerShell language spec §2.2.3), the subexpression scan shares the top-level lexer, ownership needs the repository suffix, and the Windows test spawns each hook at its own timeout. The seat added five breaks for these (27–31); all are caught.

**Final reviews, round 2.** sol (7/10) and astra (90/100) closed round 1 and sent it back once more. sol found `<#` opening a block comment inside a word (`issue<#123` hid a live commit), the same class as round 1's `#`. Both found evidence gaps: R-1055's new doctor cases uncited, R-1056 without an existing outside-checkout target, R-1060 not proving doctor never runs `claude`, R-937's skipped rows counted rather than named. Build 5 closed all of it with one boundary rule for `#` and `<#`; the seat added break 32 (37 of 37 caught). astra's nested block-comment case is a parse error in PowerShell, whose block comments do not nest (spec §2.2.3; inferred, not run), so nothing executes.

**Final reviews, round 3.** astra LAND-WITH-FIXES (94/100) on two evidence references; sol SEND-BACK (8/10): the boundary predicate held only part of the set its own cited spec names, so a `#` right after a closing quote was missed and a `)` inside that comment closed `$( … )` early. Build 6 made the set the spec's union and fixed the references. The confirmation round ran over the three-round cap with the standard reason.

**Windows CI.** On build 6's code (run 38347800159, Windows job 115133128863) the Windows leg runs the new exec-form test file green (25 checks), including a real spawn of each installed entry at its own 5 s timeout; the pipe guard (84) and the forced-Windows doctor file (86) pass in that same job. Build 5's run (38342945583) had shown 25, 69 and 86 before build 6 added the boundary cases. Builds 4 and 5 each had one Windows-only test-fixture bug (backslash paths the ownership check could not read), caught by that leg. Still red there and outside this lane: three file-mode checks, a test that deletes its own working folder, and the knowledge and adoption files the triage lists. From 2026-10-12 23:00Z the macOS and Linux legs are red for an upstream reason: pi-codemode 1.2.0 breaks fresh installs of pi 1.0.2 for code that imports pi's modules; the local locked suite is this lane's macOS evidence, and a separate urgent lane pins CI's pi install.

**Your machine check (Owner).** Step by step, in PowerShell, with a throwaway folder: `docs/reviews/cc-hooks-windows-2026-10-12/owner-windows-check.md`. It is the only check of Claude Code's own spawn of exec-form hooks, `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`'s form, PowerShell routing and hook latency.

**Lessons.** (1) Every "stays" clause in a plan needs its own code break: the 24 planned breaks covered only new behaviour, and the regression hit kept behaviour. (2) A seat fixture that stands for an installer entry must look like one; the seat's seed hid half the regression for a round. (3) Instructions for the owner are a deliverable: astra sent back "pipe a test run before a commit" as unrunnable, so the check is now a page of exact commands. (4) After a builder refactors, re-run the whole mutation table: the seat re-ran only its new breaks and missed that two older anchors had moved. (5) A hand-written lexer for another shell gets a differential test against that shell's own tokenizer, not character-by-character review: three rounds each found one more boundary character.
