## 2026-10-11 — the pi seat installs on Windows; the owner's process rulings

Spend served the current priority: the pi seat on Windows is the owner's daily environment, and the first Windows CI run found its install never registered nana with pi.

**The change.** On Windows, install and doctor run the first supported pi on PATH: `pi.com`, `.exe`, `.bat` or `.cmd`, in PATHEXT order. Node cannot start a `.cmd` shim without a shell, so a shim runs through cmd.exe with `/d /v:off /s /c` and each argument in double quotes. A shim whose path or arguments hold a character cmd.exe cannot carry is refused, not run. A pi that is found but cannot start, or fails its version check, is now a problem that fails install, on every platform — except that on macOS and Linux a `pi` whose interpreter is missing still reads as not installed, because the system reports it the same way. Post-edit reports a missing Windows tool as "could not run" by the rule cross-spawn uses (exit 1 and a command nothing resolves), never by cmd.exe's localised text.

**Plan and build.** sol reviewed the plan five times. Version 1 found pi through npm's global folder, which misses pnpm, Volta and Scoop; version 2 looks on PATH, as the terminal does. Later rounds sharpened which characters to refuse, how doctor reports a refusal, and a conservative post-edit rule. Three luna rounds built it. Two Windows CI runs then corrected the seat's own test design: on the hosted runner Git's `date.exe`, `dir.exe` and `echo.exe` sit on PATH, and no cmd.exe internal command's help exits 0, so the probe now checks help text on stdout instead. An old POSIX-only test also crashed the file before the new Windows test could run. The final reviews then asked for stronger evidence and one safer test: the Windows shim test now stops before registration unless its own fixture was installed and selected, and refuses to launch any other pi. On the last Windows run the lane's four test files pass: the command helpers, pi registration (including a real npm-generated shim that receives a folder named with a space and `& ( ) ^ ;` intact), post-edit status, and doctor runtime, whose POSIX-only probes now skip on Windows. The seat's 18 code mutations all turn a cross-platform test red.

**The owner's process rulings.** A workflow audit of six lanes counted 86 extra rounds, of which 15 caught a real bug: 19 chased rare cases outside any real threat, 23 were builder misses, 14 real design bugs, 11 seat mistakes, 7 empty tests found late. The owner accepted all four recommendations: name the threat in every plan (honest variation in, forgery out); cap plan reviews at one round for small lanes and two for gate or format lanes, and edit nothing once every reviewer says LAND; ship urgent fixes alone; time one lane each with Sonnet 5.5 and luna before changing builders. The owner's Windows machine is x64 with Git Bash.

**Correction to the verdict-reader entry below.** It says the seat's commit during astra's first review voided that round. The ledger shows the verdict was recorded valid: the commit touched only the review-records folder, which the reviewed-tree check leaves out.

**Lessons.** (1) Measure the runner before designing a probe around it; two CI runs went to assumptions about cmd.exe nobody had checked. (2) Find the prior art before the first plan: cross-spawn, already installed with pi, held both launch rules.

## 2026-10-11 — the verdict reader: first-line verdicts, so yokai-world lands again

Spend served the current priority: the land rule is one of its appetite items, and a fault in it blocked another product. The owner relayed a yokai-world session: "I merged by hand. The merge helper refused, because the review tool logged no verdict for any round. … That is a toolkit fault to fix." The land rule read the verdict only from a review's final line. yokai-world's reviewers write it first, with a bare score, so nine rounds recorded nothing and every land was refused.

**Plan.** The seat scanned every review output the ledger names (338 of 364 still exist) and yokai-world's reviews (76 with the verdict first only). Of the 338, 265 end with the verdict, 53 start with it, 12 do both, and 8 hold it only in the middle. The rule: read the final line when it carries the label; otherwise read the first line, but only a plain verdict line, and only when no other line mentions a verdict; refuse when a first-line label and the final verdict disagree. sol reviewed the plan four times (4, 5 and 7 out of 10, then LAND at 10). Each round closed a way to mask a rejection: a backtick-quoted first line, a malformed first-line rejection above a clean final LAND, invisible characters or look-alike letters hiding a label, and a check applied in one branch only. Every check that looks for a label now reads one canonical form of the line; every check that accepts a verdict reads the raw line.

**Build.** Four luna rounds and one review round. Round 1 passed the seat's 64 cases and matched the seat's prototype on all 414 corpus files. The seat's code mutations then found suite gaps twice (dropping Unicode normalisation, then the fold after normalisation and the final-line bare score); rounds 2 and 4 added those tests. The first final reviews both sent it back. sol found the first line checked by the looser final-line grammar, so a quoted or bold first-line verdict above a final LAND recorded LAND. astra found a look-alike in the reader's own table (a Greek lunate sigma) that normalisation turns into a letter the table does not fold, so a disguised rejection recorded LAND; the seat's prototype had the same flaw, so agreement with it could not catch it. Round 3 fixed both: the first line is always held to the plain form, and the table folds before and after normalisation, with a test that every entry reaches its target letter. Two seat errors were also caught before the build: a count of 129 yokai-world files that matched no real file set, and a plan claim that one existing case would stay empty. The seat also committed during astra's first review, which voided that round's verdict.

**Lessons.** (1) A format other repos write needs a scan of every repo that writes it; the land-rule scan covered three. (2) Pin a cross-repo count to a commit; a live repo moves. (3) Run every existing test case through a prototype before the build, so the brief names exactly which expectations change. (4) A prototype that shares the product's flaw cannot find it; the reviewers' adversarial probes did. (5) Never commit into a branch while a reviewer is reading it.

## 2026-10-11 — Windows in CI: the first hosted run and its triage

Spend served the current priority: Windows in CI and the fixes it finds are its next appetite items. The owner asked why CI did not cover Windows; it never had (the matrix was macOS and Linux). He approved a parallel lane and a draft pull request (#1) so CI could run the new leg before any merge.

**The change.** The suite matrix adds `windows-latest`, non-blocking like Linux, with bash as the job shell; macOS stays the blocking leg the release needs (R-1031, R-1032). The support line, one exact string in the three front doors, now says Linux and Windows run in hosted CI with non-blocking legs (R-684). sol's plan review insisted the leg reach `npm test`, not merely finish; it did on the first run.

**What Windows found.** The first run: 63 of 133 test files pass. A measurement run with LF checkout passed 68, so line endings explain only a few. A read-only triage (eight classifiers and a synthesis) sorted the 64 failing files into five product bugs a Windows user hits today — the pi seat's install never registers nana with pi (a bare spawn cannot launch npm's `pi.cmd`), scaffolded TypeScript projects break under default CRLF checkouts, `nana-setup project` fails to refresh AGENTS.md (suspected cause: replacing a file it still holds open), the knowledge hook's stale-path migration is dead, and post-edit misreports a missing tool — plus the declared gap that the Claude Code seat gets only the knowledge hook on Windows. Most other failures are test portability (`.pathname` imports, HOME without USERPROFILE, NTFS-illegal names), and they hide about seventy checks that never ran. The desk's seventeen failing files are recorded only, under its freeze. Record: `docs/reviews/windows-ci-2026-10-11/windows-triage.md`.

**Lessons.** (1) A hosted run on a draft pull request is the cheap way to see a platform before merging. (2) Measure a suspected cause before acting on it: CRLF looked like the main problem and explained five files.

## 2026-10-10 — the land rule: nothing reaches main unless every reviewer accepted it

Spend served the current priority: the land rule is its third appetite item. The owner ruled: "anything landed on main should be accepted by an independent reviewer." Until now `nana-land` landed commits no review covered (it only printed them), took a free-text `--exempt` reason instead of reviews, and read only the FIRST verdict recorded on a revision. A seat fact-check of the live ledger found 17 revisions with two verdicts; in 8 the first was LAND and a later one was not, and 6 would have landed. One was this day's four-digit ID lane, held by hand.

**Plan.** Fable's consult replaced "a review's record rides the next change" with "nothing is written after a land". A seat workflow (four read-only checkers and a critic) then checked the plan against the code and found 16 errors, among them a scope that excluded the ledger code the fix lives in. sol reviewed the plan five times (4, 5, 6, 7, then LAND-WITH-FIXES at 9 out of 10). Each round closed a real hole: a race between the last reading and the merge, an echoed format line read as LAND, a separate clone with its own records, rejections lost before the change, old code in another worktree, marks inside the verdict word, and in-flight reviews of a snapshot.

**What it does.** The round records keep every completed verdict at tally version 2; old code refuses that tally, so it fails closed. A land needs a verified version-2 LAND for each named revision, and refuses when any verified verdict at that commit — any item, or a snapshot of it — is not LAND, when a review of it is in flight, when a commit is not covered, when the source and main are not one repository, or when an option other than the four it knows is passed. Its last reading runs under the ledger lock through the merge. The verdict is read from the final non-blank line, which must be a verdict line in the strict form (markdown marks only before the label or around its parts) by a pattern taken from every real verdict line in the review corpus. The helper prints no HANDOFF or session text. The owner's checkpoint 1: the every-verdict row also applies to the merge feature, whose purpose now reads "integrate only changes every reviewer accepted".

**Build.** Ten luna rounds. Round 1 got the behaviour right but deleted 36 of the 37 land tests (they used the retired option) and pointed eleven rows at one suite test that ran the seat's own acceptance script. The seat added a title-coverage check and split the rest into short checklist rounds; every test came back on reviewed fixtures, each new row got tests that pin it, and the old rows got their exact evidence back. The seat's own run of 15 mutation pairs then found four review-ledger tests whose bodies never ran: a function was passed to a check that takes true or false, so each printed PASS. Build 7 made them run and made that check refuse a function; all 15 pairs now turn their named test red. astra's land review then found that an annotated tag object named as the reviewed revision landed, and that the README missed four declared limits; build 8 fixed both, and moved the post-merge checks and release status back outside the ledger lock. sol's first review stalled on pi-review's 75-second watchdog while running long tests. Its second found that the new parser looked only at lines that START with the label, so `VERDICT: LAND` followed by `Correction: VERDICT: SEND-BACK` recorded LAND; build 9 takes the last line carrying the label anywhere, then applies the strict pattern. The old code showed the same class live: it took the FIRST verdict line, so sol's own SEND-BACK review, which quoted that example mid-text, was recorded as LAND, and the old helper would have accepted the revision. The seat read both reviews and held it. sol's third review found two more paths (a fenced example after the final verdict, and a non-English prefix such as `拒否:`), so build 10 reads only the final non-blank line, with an explicit set of marks allowed before the label. Records: `docs/reviews/land-rule-2026-10-10/`.

**Lessons.** (1) A read-only fact-check workflow before the first plan review found what three sol rounds would have. (2) A builder blocked by an old test deletes it; guard every lane with a title-coverage check and the suite's check count. (3) luna completes about three items of a long brief per round; give it a checklist of three. (4) A green suite is not proof a test runs: the seat's mutation pairs are what showed four tests checked nothing.

## 2026-10-09/10 — the requirements tree and four-digit IDs (one merge); the owner's rulings and the new priority

Spend served the current priority: the tree and four-digit IDs are its first two appetite items. The loop was the owner's new feature process: why, plan, Fable consult, sol plan review, `pi-worker --lane` build, seat verification, sol build review, astra land review, the owner's checkpoint, land.

**The tree.** the owner asked for the requirements as a capability → feature → subgroup tree he can read; the seat first argued against it from an overlap metric and was corrected (shared feedback memory). Increment B ran one placement review over all 1,009 rows (17 moved), let a row apply to more than one feature (113 shares over 95 rows in 30 features, flagged as high blast radius), and added feature lifecycle statuses. Reviews found a compressor that dropped the second ID of two-ID runs (74 IDs), G IDs rendered as R, heading forms the checker missed, a field check that called the renderer it checked, and a placeholder bypass that a builder report claimed fixed until the seat re-ran it. Records: `docs/reviews/req-tree-2026-10-09/`.

**Four-digit IDs.** R-1000 accepts three ASCII digits or four not starting with zero in rows and `req:` markers; R-1001 makes a reserved-prefix line that is not a valid row fail, naming file and line. Three sol plan rounds fixed Unicode digits, missed consumers and undefined fences. Six build rounds then made the two rails, and the tree checker, read the same file the same way: CRLF and trailing whitespace (sol and astra r1); one line definition (the seat: the TypeScript rail silently dropped a row holding U+2028); one explicit whitespace list plus one byte-order-mark rule (sol r2); a byte-order mark removed exactly once per file, and the tree checker on the rail's whitespace (sol and astra r3); and the tree counting a row only through the rail's own row test (sol r4). The seat chose the union of both languages' whitespace over sol's ASCII-only fix, which would have hidden rows both rails read today. Records: `docs/reviews/req-ids-2026-10-10/`; the final review verdicts live in the review ledger.

**Seat decisions at checkpoint 2.** The seven desk features stay frozen, now citing the owner's 2026-10-10 ruling. R-224 keeps its share with the display feature: that feature owns the single renderer R-224 requires, so a renderer change must keep the knowledge pull's pointer fields escaped. R-1000 and R-1001 also apply to project setup, whose templates ship both rails.

**The owner's rulings (2026-10-10), from the product decision report** (a published page built from the ledger): nothing reaches main unless an independent reviewer accepted it, so this merge carries its own notes and nothing is written after it; rm may run unasked only on plain targets strictly inside the working directory; the owner requires Windows testing now, CI first, a UTM Windows 11 VM next; the desk stays frozen; a pi extension's default export counts as its named entry point; a study stops when it cannot write its evidence. The new priority line in the umbrella `OBJECTIVE.md` landed after a sol LAND. The owner asked for the product report to become a feature (plan drafted, after Fable) and lifted the HTML-page hold.

**Lessons.** (1) A line-oriented parser shared by two languages needs one written definition of a line, of whitespace and of a byte-order mark, and the same cases run through both. (2) The review log keeps the first verdict per revision only, so two reviewers on one revision can mask a rejection. It happened in round 4: astra's LAND was recorded first, sol's SEND-BACK only in the audit log, and the land helper would have merged; the seat held the merge. The land-rule lane fixes it. (3) A brief that demands verbatim output and a short report gets a summary; have the builder write the output to a committed file.

**Found on the machine.** The Codex app re-imports the legacy skills into `~/.agents/skills` each night; leaked test processes (a desk test server alive 29 hours) were killed; the objective-golden timing flake recurred under load.

**Lessons.** (1) Probe a tool's behaviour before a ruling depends on it (git `update-ref` then `merge --ff-only` leaves files stale; `node --check` rejects TypeScript). (2) A guard hook abstains on a miss; `allow` is a permission grant. (3) Subtract exemptions on a floor rather than refining them — it converged twice this tranche. (4) Proportional stopping: on low-risk lanes, rare edge cases after three rounds become declared residuals. (5) Brief one item per round when a builder stops early; "wrong code first" and "fix the class" are now in the preamble.

## 2026-10-05 — the edge desk on pi's built-in MCP; the lock-file advice

Spend served the current priority: it removed the last pi-mcp-adapter consumer and closed a `violated` row. Roles: Sonnet worker in two worktrees, gpt-6-astra through `pi-review`, the seat (Opus 5.5) briefed, verified and landed.

**Lock-file advice.** R-760 was `violated`: it forbade "move it aside" for an obstructed lock as well as a held one. The code was right. An obstructed lock path is never a running pi's lock, and pi never clears it. The seat narrowed the row and pinned it by mutation. astra r1 then found a real unsafe case behind it: a genuinely held proper-lockfile lock acquired under a restrictive umask is unreadable (mode 333), and nana called it obstructed and advised moving it. Fixed (staleness decides; an unreadable fresh folder is held). astra r2 found the new remedies claimed more than the check knows. A stale unreadable empty folder is reclaimed by pi, yet the advice said pi fails. Fixed with uncertainty-aware remedies (R-856/R-857), with the readable remedies byte-identical over 144 combinations.

**Edge desk.** The probe found the brief's argv could not work: `--no-extensions` disables pi's built-in extensions too, so a server registered from `-e` never connects. `-e builtin:mcp` (pi's own grammar) fixes it. The worker built past the brief's stop condition; the seat accepted it because it is documented pi behaviour and kept the trust posture. The app's own extension registers the server, as basketball does. Blocks now arrive at `structuredContent.structuredContent.blocks`. nana-stage reads them there and drops the raw carrier by never returning `structuredContent`; the adapter path and its overflow branch are gone. The desk accepts `builtin:<name>` extension entries (R-943/R-944). astra r1 BLOCK 7 → r2 BLOCK 8 → r3 LAND 9. Live: the quiesce-first runbook, then a real prompt staged two signed blocks with no raw carrier.

**Lessons.** (1) A wrapper log redirected into the reviewed tree voids the round: the snapshot changes mid-review (memory updated). (2) A running service that caches config at load needs a stop before the checkout changes, not a restart after: astra showed a mixed old-manifest/new-stage window. (3) `launchctl bootstrap` loaded the desk without starting it; `kickstart` started it. (4) A classification fix can make a remedy overclaim: test the advice text, not just the label.

**Review.** gpt-5.6-sol r1 (adversarial) BLOCK: CRITICAL the win32 skill mirror followed a directory symlink and wrote into its target; HIGH adopt mode shipped a false ledger with no rail; HIGH "every module" mapped only src; MEDIUM nested tests invisible, implemented without a citation, Python dynamic imports silent. All fixed by two fixers with mutation proofs (victim byte-identical; adopt rows all untested; header drop in tests/ red; nested unknown id red; evidence `—` red; non-literal import named). Friction: the reviewer wrote the `--out` file itself and the wrapper overwrote it with the final message — body recovered from the pi session jsonl; procedure memory updated (never instruct the reviewer to write the file).

**Self-hosting.** Three read-only extraction passes (pack+runner 258 rows, knowledge/stage/setup 108, desk/bench 103) → `REQUIREMENTS.md` 481 rows, 499 after the clause audit; the pack's overflow block moved to R-700+ before publication. Three header passes over 70 modules (one `*/` inside a header value broke the test runner — caught by `node --check`, now fixed); three bench modules exempt (content-pinned by a closed study; re-pinning would alter committed evidence). Markers placed mechanically on 1,130 `check(` calls (the rail had to learn mid-line calls and `check` as a call name). Wiring worker: shims over the template modules, root map config (two layers), `docs/code-map.md` 73 modules (162 once the six test roots were mapped after r2), README check over seven READMEs — 380 first-run problems, ~360 of them extraction errors (machine paths, package specifiers, README-relative paths) → classifier fixed to the spec's words, README-dir resolution, `externalPaths` declared with reasons; the remaining real README errors fixed one by one (listed in the worker report; nana-stage README written). Four repo-level tests under `npm test` (rail, map, README, and an external test of the runner itself). **Sol r2 BLOCK** (inline README commands unchecked — 443 → 506 claims; implemented rows overclaiming clauses — a three-worker clause audit of all 416 implemented rows: 136 re-cited to the check that pins the clause, 17 split; `npm test` red under an ambient `NANA_HANDOFF=off` — the runner now scrubs `NANA_*`/`PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` from children; test roots unmapped — headers on 89 test modules, map 73 → 162). Full suite 83 → 89 files, 5,174 → 5,454 checks, green.

**Lessons.** (1) A reviewer told to "write the file" loses its review to the wrapper; capture the final message. (2) A header is code: a `*/` in a value closes the comment — syntax-check after a comments-only pass. (3) A README checker's first run is mostly its own extraction errors; fix classification to the spec's words before touching READMEs, and declare the genuine externals with reasons rather than weakening the check. (4) Three disjoint lanes → one independent reviewer → one fixer per finding set held up across 200+ files; the ledger is where workers overclaim, never the code — 58 of 85 sampled desk/bench rows had an unmarked adjacent check that pinned the missing clause: marker placement, not missing tests. (5) Never edit the reviewed tree while pi-review runs — r2's verdict was voided by my own HANDOFF edit and the round was consumed.

**r3 (last round): BLOCK on one class** — clause-level overclaim persists (fresh sample 16/25 fully pinned) while every round-1/2 fix re-verified. Landed with the residual recorded in REQUIREMENTS 6b and HANDOFF; nine sampled rows split. **Open:** tag `v0.6.0` for copier consumers; migrate basketball-geek's `@pytest.mark.req` to the comment marker when touched; work-project keeps its R-600 block.
